newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Transport ministers back EU hard line with Swiss.
newsitem.headline: Transport ministers back EU hard line with Swiss.

text.p: European Union transport ministers have given their backing to the EU's robust stance in negotiating access for heavy vehicle traffic through Switzerland.

"No-one is in favour of a levy of 600 Swiss francs. I think it is a prohibitive levy," Dutch transport minister Annemarie Jorritsma told a news conference in Amsterdam on Friday after a one-day informal transport council.
Switzerland last week proposed a 600 Swiss franc charge per truck as the price to be paid for lifting its current ban on vehicles exceeding 28 tonnes.
The EU wants Switzerland to allow in 40 tonne trucks which currently take diversions through France and Austria for journeys through the Alps.
European Transport Commissioner Neil Kinnock said he respected the arithmetic of the Swiss, but reiterated his statement of last week that the proposed charge was prohibitive.
"Six hundred Swiss francs for crossing Switzerland is not even a figure to start talking about," he said.
EU ministers nevertheless agreed that a resolution of the dispute was a matter of urgency.
"We are looking for a satisfactory agreement in the early months of this year," Kinnock said.

He said Friday's ministerial meeting had produce a range of ideas that should comfort Swiss sensitivities, but would not give details, saying it would be inappropriate to reveal the EU's hand at this stage.
"We're not very much inclined to go into great detail as ... that would spoil the nice surprises we have for them," Kinnock said.
Earlier on Friday, Jorritsma briefly met a delegation of environmental protestors, complaining about the EU's pressure on the Swiss government.

A grouping of European environmental bodies calling itself 'Platform to Another Europe' sited a 10 metre high inflatable mountain, representative of the threatened Swiss Alps, in Amsterdam's central Dam square.
Transport ministers also agreed that member countries should proceed with haste in settling upon a common system of electronic road tolls.
"A certain degree of urgency is required... The point simply is to avoid the incompatibility we saw (in the development) of televisions ..(or) mobile phones," Jorritsma said.
Kinnock added that while countries would not be forced to adopt road tolls, those that decided to do so would be urged to adopt the common system.
"The fact that some countries are already operating (a given toll system) will not mean that they be excluded from an interoperable system," he said.
On Saturday, the informal committee will conclude with talks on air traffic management, the third issue on the Dutch agenda.
The two-day informal council comes under the aegis of the Netherlands' six month presidency of the European Union.
The Dutch themselves reinforced their EU credentials at the start of the council by unveiling new national car licence plates and road signs, each with a European flavour.
The innovations are intended as an example for rest of Europe to copy.
